A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DINCO research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments can be matched reliably, including v1 Tables 7–8, which become v2 Tables 10–11.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration experiments on TriviaQA, SimpleQA, and biography generation, together with suggestibility, sampling-budget, saturation, and NLI-ablation results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds biomedical QA experiments, larger-model evaluation, sensitivity analyses, distractor statistics, and an efficiency-variant comparison.

M1.justification: Appendix D.7 introduces a one-step variant that validates each distractor through a follow-up correctness turn in the same conversation, replacing separate generation and validation calls. The original normalization, NLI weighting, and equal combination of self-consistency and normalized confidence remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix D.6 adds BioASQ14 factoid evaluation requiring biomedical expertise, substantially extending coverage beyond general factual questions and biographies. TriviaQA, SimpleQA, and biography generation remain; the additional analyses on those datasets do not themselves introduce new task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmark comparisons retain VC, K-VC, MSP, SC-VC, and SC, with the same applicable subset for biography generation. The added Qwen3-32B and BioASQ comparisons reuse these methods. Correcting K-VC's citation and identifying MSP as the strongest average-ECE baseline do not change comparator membership.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen3-32B, comparisons across four NLI checkpoints, and budgets of 8, 12, and 16 with varied self-consistency/distractor allocations (Appendices D.3–D.6). BioASQ uses 1,000 factoid questions from its Task B training set. The original experiments retain their splits, metrics, and default budget.

E4.justification: v2 adds distractor case studies and attribute analyses (C.1), extends the suggestibility analysis to SimpleQA and biographies (D.1), tests NLI-checkpoint and budget-allocation sensitivity (D.3–D.4), and compares one-step versus two-step execution (D.7). These substantially expand validation of the method's components and practical tradeoffs beyond v1's existing ablations.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly uses kernel density estimation for joint distractor-attribute distributions, a limited addition to statistical estimation. The existing 10,000-resample ECE/BS procedures and one-sided DeLong test remain unchanged in the renumbered significance-testing appendix; no new repeated-run uncertainty reporting is introduced.

E6.justification: The retained result tables have unchanged numerical entries, but v2 adds substantial results for distractor properties, sensitivity, efficiency, Qwen3-32B, and BioASQ. Newly reported DINCO ECE is 0.065 on Qwen3-32B TriviaQA and 0.071 on BioASQ (Tables 13 and 15). The TriviaQA summary changes from a 0.099 advantage over SC to 0.077 over MSP, correcting the comparison rather than demonstrating a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Section 2.3 adds an idealized invariance argument: with fully equivalent or contradictory claims, uniqueness weights become reciprocal equivalence-class sizes, yielding duplication invariance, while contradiction weights neutralize inclusion of the original claim. The original bias assumptions, normalization derivation, and equations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central suggestibility, calibration, saturation, and sampling-efficiency claims. The introduction narrows the reported TriviaQA advantage from 0.099 to 0.077 ECE, consistent with Section 3.2's corrected identification of MSP as the best average-ECE baseline.

C2.justification: Appendix C.1 substantially expands the reasoning about model-relative distractor plausibility, potentially factual distractors, and NLI reliability in specialized domains. Section 4 qualifies budget matching by acknowledging 32% greater FLOP cost. Appendix D.7 explains API restrictions on the cheaper variant, while smaller-model distractor generation is explicitly presented as untested.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the one-step validation prompt, additional NLI checkpoint identifiers and parameter counts, and FLOP accounting. It identifies the human evaluator as one author and updates the code pointer from dubai03nsr/dinco to victorwang37/dinco. Existing prompts and implementation descriptions largely remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds the BioASQ citation and connects possible smaller-model distractor generation to Li et al.'s contrastive decoding. K-VC is reattributed to the already-cited Tian et al. (2023), and the Tian et al. (2024) reference is removed. The broader positioning against joint confidence prompting and prior coherence methods is retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. v2 refines explanations and result summaries, expands and subdivides the appendices, updates cross-references, and adds a conference header and acknowledgments. This is targeted editing and organizational expansion rather than a comprehensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds distractor-example tables, correlation and density displays, sensitivity plots, and benchmark and efficiency tables. Figure 3 gains cumulative distributions and mean markers; Figure 4 gains FLOP annotations and an expanded caption. Existing tables are redistributed, and the numerical-confidence tables are retained as Tables 10–11.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for DINCO by examining previously untested distractor quality, NLI-checkpoint sensitivity, and budget allocation. It also corrects the strongest-baseline comparison and replaces an implication of equal compute with explicit FLOP accounting. These changes improve experimental credibility and practical interpretability. One qualification remains: Table 16's claim of calibration parity is too broad because the cheaper variant has worse Brier scores and AUC, but this does not outweigh the stronger validation and transparency.
